A radical is a chemical entity, typically an atom or molecule, that has an 
unpaired electron. This electron is commonly shown as a dot (+). For example, 
chlorine and methyl radicals are represented as Cl- and -CH,, respectively. 
Radicals are formed by homolytic fission of covalent bonds, which involves 
the breaking of the bonding electron pair and the movement of individual 
electrons in opposite directions. In reaction mechanisms, this type of electron 
movement is shown by single-barbed (fish-hook) arrows (figure 8).

Radical substitution in alkanes 
At low temperatures, alkanes are relatively unreactive because all C—C and 
C—H bonds in their molecules are strong and almost non-polar. However, 
alkanes participate in radical substitution (SR) reactions with halogens. These 
reactions are initiated by ultraviolet (UV) light or heat and involve initiation, 
propagation and termination steps.

Note that the combination of two alkyl radicals produces a new alkane 
(in this case, ethane) with twice as many carbon atoms as the original 
molecule. Halogenation of ethane under similar conditions would 
produce butane. 
Radical bromination of alkanes proceeds in the same way as radical 
chlorination. Fluorine is too reactive, so direct fluorination of alkanes often 
leads to the breaking of carbon-carbon bonds and the formation of a complex 
mixture of products. The reactivity of iodine is too low, so radical iodination of 
alkanes does not occur.

Similarities: In both cases a covalent bond breaks, and the electron pair is no longer shared between two atoms. In both cases, a single molecule (or other species) breaks up into two species. Both processes are endothermic.
Differences: In homolytic fission, the bond breaks symmetrically and the two electrons of the shared pair move in opposite directions, so each atom receives a single electron. In heterolytic fission, the bond breaks non-symmetrically and both electrons of the shared pair move in one direction, so one atom receives both electrons while the other atom receives none. Homolytic fission produces uncharged species (two radicals) while heterolytic fission produces charged species (a cation and an anion).
Reaction type: radical substitution (SR). Conditions: UV light or heat.
Depending on the reaction temperature, all participating species can be liquid or gaseous. In reaction mechanisms, the states are optional.
